response.description_long:
Serverless GPU platforms have long forced a binary choice on their users: keep expensive GPUs warm around the clock and pay for idle capacity, or accept cold starts of a minute or more while containers pull, weights load, CUDA initializes, and kernels warm. Modelgrid's entire pitch is that this tradeoff is artificial. The company runs machine-learning models as autoscaling API endpoints and claims restores of under two seconds even for models tens of gigabytes in size, which it says dissolves the choice between paying for idle GPUs and making users wait.

The mechanism is a snapshot architecture. A conventional cold start replays an initialization sequence that is serial at every step — pull the container, load weights from object storage, initialize CUDA, allocate memory, warm the kernels — and Modelgrid's argument is that none of that work is the model's fault. So the platform runs the sequence once at deploy time and freezes the result: process memory, device state, and the allocator's arena layout. That snapshot lives in a distributed cache on NVMe within the same rack as the GPUs it will restore to, making a restore a memory map and a device-state replay rather than a download. Restores are deterministic, which the company says makes scale-out uniform: the tenth replica comes up as fast as the first. New model versions get their snapshot built and validated before traffic shifts, so a bad deploy does not take down the running version.

The platform handles anything with a PyTorch or vLLM serving path: language models, embedding models, diffusion models, speech-to-text. Users bring a container or a Python function; Modelgrid manages batching, queueing, autoscaling from zero, and GPU selection. For vLLM workloads, continuous batching and paged attention come pre-configured — the user sets a model id and context length. For custom PyTorch, a Python SDK wraps a predict function and infers batching behavior from its signature. Streaming responses, server-sent events, and long-running jobs up to 30 minutes work on every endpoint. GPU classes span A100 (40 GB and 80 GB configurations) and H100, with multi-GPU serving on H100 nodes with NVLink for models that shard across devices.

Autoscaling follows queue depth and latency targets rather than fixed warm pools. Users set a p95 target and a maximum queue time, and the scheduler decides when a burst justifies restoring another replica — a decision the company says only works because a restore costs two seconds, not two minutes. Idle replicas drain after a configurable window, and scale-to-zero means an idle deployed model costs nothing. Batch and scheduled work run on the same endpoints: submit a job array, and the scheduler fans it across restored replicas before scaling back down.

The billing model is per-second, metered on compute time only. Queue time is free, snapshot storage is free for active endpoints, and restore and idle time are not billed. The published rate card starts at $2.10 per hour equivalent for A100 40 GB, $3.10 for A100 80 GB, and $5.60 for H100, billed by the second with volume discounts at sustained usage. There are no minimums or reservations, though reserved capacity exists for teams wanting guaranteed headroom. A worked example in the docs makes the economics concrete: an embedding endpoint on an A100 40 GB serving 10 minutes of traffic a day meters roughly 6 GPU-hours a month, against 720 for the always-warm alternative.

Modelgrid was founded in San Francisco in 2023 by Ilya Sorokin and Grace Tan, infrastructure engineers from a large GPU cloud where they watched customers pay for idle GPUs to avoid cold starts they could not fix. The founding bet is architectural — cold starts are a consequence of replaying initialization that could have been saved, not a fact of physics — and the company argues that owning the serving stack from the rack to the scheduler is what makes the restore path fast enough to change the economics. That is also why it runs its own capacity in three US regions rather than reselling serverless on top of a hyperscaler, where placement would belong to someone else's algorithm. Each endpoint deploys across at least two regions with health-based routing and automatic failover, cross-region failover is exercised weekly by internal chaos tests, and private networking connects a customer VPC to endpoints without traversing the public internet. Endpoints support IP allowlists and per-tenant encryption keys for weights and snapshots, workloads run in isolated VMs with dedicated GPU attachment, and the company is SOC 2 Type II certified.

Transparency is unusually central to the pitch. The status page publishes live p50 and p95 restore times by model-size bucket alongside per-region API latency, uptime history goes back to launch, and incident reports are described as unedited. Observability ships with every endpoint: request latency broken into queue, restore, and compute time; token throughput for vLLM endpoints; per-replica GPU memory and utilization; Prometheus and Datadog export; and metered seconds per endpoint per day on the dashboard. The site does not name specific customers or disclose revenue or funding figures, so traction claims here rest on the published mechanics and pricing rather than named logos. Snapshots are validated for models up to 140 GB today, and the company says it is hiring systems engineers for CUDA runtime, storage, and scheduler roles.
